item.title: Crude bomb explosions reported in Jatrabari
item.description:
Several crude bombs exploded at an intersection in Jatrabari early Sunday, triggering panic among residents. No casualties or injuries were reported.
The explosions occurred shortly after 1am, according to police.
Sub-Inspector Salauddin, duty officer at Jatrabari police station, confirmed the incident.
He said police were investigating the explosions and reviewing CCTV footage from the surrounding area.
“Preliminary information suggests that two people riding a motorcycle detonated several crude bombs before fleeing the scene. We are working to identify and apprehend them,” he said.
Witnesses said they heard three to four explosions in quick succession at the Jatrabari intersection, prompting panic among people in the area. Police arrived shortly afterwards.

item.title: Sovereign AI ambition meets technical reality
item.description:
The government’s ambition to build a sovereign "Bangla Large Language Model (LLM)" has gained renewed momentum within official policymaking circles.
Spearheaded by the ICT Division and administrative stakeholders, the state plan envisions setting up high-performance computing nodes centered at the National Data Center in Kaliakair, supported by eight regional data centers across divisional headquarters.
The state's rationale frames local model development as a prerequisite for digital sovereignty, cultural preservation, and linguistic inclusion.
However, tech industry analysts, machine learning researchers, and software architects are raising critical questions about the technical premises and financial feasibility of state-funded foundational AI model creation.
While public narrative frequently treats AI models as discrete, language-bound software systems, modern foundational engineering reveals a very different landscape—one where direct government intervention risks creating a costly, redundant public asset rather than a useful technological utility.
In machine learning architecture, language-bound AI is a conceptual contradiction.
Neural networks do not process human vocabulary, syntax, or grammar in isolation; they function by converting input tokens into multi-dimensional vector embeddings within a shared mathematical concept space.
Modern foundational architectures process semantic logic, contextual connections, and structural patterns across dozens of human languages simultaneously.
State-funded plans to create a brand-new foundational model exclusively for Bangla misinterpret how global models function.
Frontier LLMs do not need to be rebuilt from scratch to comprehend Bengali. Massive open-source models—ranging from 24 billion to 64 billion parameters—already exist freely in the global developer ecosystem.
These platforms have already ingested vast swathes of open-web Bengali text during their multi-trillion-token pre-training phases.
Replicating this core architecture domestically adds zero foundational value while requiring computational infrastructure that costs billions of dollars—a scale of ongoing capital expenditure visible in the quarterly financial reports of global technology conglomerates like Google, Meta, and Anthropic.
Grounded integration
A significant volume of Bengali knowledge remains outside the digital realm—confined to printed literature, historical manuscripts, regional archives, and library collections across the country.
However, digitizing this material does not necessitate training a new foundation model from scratch.
To incorporate offline archives, the industry standard is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
Under a RAG pipeline, physical documents are scanned, digitized, vectorized, and stored in a searchable database.
When a user asks a question, the system retrieves relevant historical context from local records and feeds it directly into an existing open-source LLM.
This delivers domain-specific accuracy without altering the underlying model parameters.
Similarly, regional accents and localized spoken dialects—such as Noakhali, Chattogram, or Sylheti—require targeted speech-to-text (STT) and fine-tuning datasets rather than foundational architecture redesigns.
Extending existing models to handle local vocal nuances is an incremental fine-tuning layer, not a ground-up engineering task.
Administrative limits and procurement hazards
Past industrial endeavors demonstrate that direct state execution in consumer or high-tech manufacturing struggles with rapid innovation cycles.
When deep-tech initiatives fall under conventional administrative frameworks, project implementation often shifts from software engineering toward traditional bureaucracy: tenders, procurement cycles, contractor allocations, and physical infrastructure management.
Instead of yielding agile, market-ready technology, direct state management risks creating over-budget and under-utilized assets—much like previous state technology assembly initiatives that struggled to find commercial adoption against global private competition.
Lessons from Google Bard
The global evolution of Natural Language Processing (NLP) demonstrates how multi-lingual models acquire non-English capabilities natively.
When Google introduced Bard (now Gemini), computer scientists noted that the system began demonstrating fluency in low-resource languages, including Bengali, through a phenomenon known as "emergent property."
By training deep transformer layers on massive multi-lingual datasets, the model independently maps linguistic structures, semantic relationships, and cross-lingual concepts.
By anchoring low-resource data against high-resource language vectors, global models developed Bengali comprehension organically through scale rather than through isolated, localized manual programming.
Strategic alternatives
Rather than allocating capital toward building redundant core models, experts suggest a pragmatic shift in state policy:
Evaluating the state-led Bangla AI push
Category
Pros (State-Led Native Model Push)
Cons (Technical & Financial Drawbacks)
Data & Sovereignty
Direct national administrative oversight over local citizen data and public service integration.
Redundant, as open-source multi-lingual models already process public Bengali text securely on local servers.
Resource Allocation
Allocates public funding toward national technology infrastructure and local data center expansion.
High financial burden; foundational pre-training costs billions in compute, duplicating existing global open-source work.
Execution Risk
Creates a centralized government roadmap for public-sector digitalization.
Vulnerable to administrative procurement delays, tender inefficiencies, and fast technical obsolescence.
Linguistic Scope
Encourages systematic digitization of physical Bengali archives and national literary collections.
Inefficient path for software delivery; RAG pipelines and model fine-tuning achieve identical domain accuracy at a fraction of the cost.

item.title: The future of 60m button phones in Bangladesh
item.description:
The telecommunications landscape in Bangladesh is heading toward a massive structural shift. The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) has outlined a definitive roadmap to completely phase out 2G technology by December 2029.
While telecom operators have welcomed the decision as a necessary step toward modernizing digital infrastructure, the move raises serious questions about the fate of roughly 60 million traditional button phones currently in use across the country.
To ensure a managed transition away from legacy technology, BTRC has established a series of strict deadlines leading up to the final network shutdown:
Industry estimates indicate that about 65% of locally produced handsets are still basic 2G feature phones, typically priced around Tk950 to Tk1,000.
In contrast, affordable 4G smartphones generally start at a much higher price point of around Tk9,500.
Because the vast majority of existing button phones do not support VoLTE (Voice over LTE) technology, millions of low-income and rural consumers face a steep financial hurdle to stay connected once the network is retired.
Experts and local manufacturing representatives have emphasized that restricting 2G devices must be balanced with practical alternatives—such as government-backed initiatives for ultra-low-cost smartphones or accessible installment facilities—to prevent economic strain on lower-income populations and to avoid flooding the market with illegal devices.
Major mobile network operators, including Grameenphone, Robi, and Banglalink, have strongly endorsed the transition.
Industry leaders noted that retiring outdated 2G infrastructure will allow operators to redirect critical spectrum resources, significantly boost data network capacity, and deliver higher-quality mobile internet services nationwide as digital connectivity becomes the primary focus of the telecommunications sector.

West Indies focused on piling lead, not setting a target: Hodge
item.description:
CRICKET-BAN-WIS-TEST

West Indies batter Kavem Hodge said his team would continue to pile on the lead rather than set a fixed target, as they tightened their grip on the second and final Test against Bangladesh at Sylhet International Cricket Stadium today, Sunday.

Hodge, who struck an unbeaten century to put West Indies in control, said the wicket remained good for batting and the team would assess the situation before deciding how far they wanted to go on the fifth day.

“It’s a pretty good wicket. Tomorrow we’ll assess and see what’s the best score, what’s the best total, and what’s the best tempo on this wicket. But as of now, we’re just trying to keep piling on the lead,” Hodge told newspersons after the day’s play.

West Indies reached 345-3 at stumps on Day 4, stretching their overall lead to 315 runs and putting themselves in a strong position to push for a series sweep.

Hodge who was not out on 140 said his century was particularly satisfying as he managed to contribute at a crucial stage after failing to make a significant impact in the opening Test in Dhaka.

“I got a start in the first game in Dhaka, but obviously I didn’t get the results that I would have loved to. It’s always nice to contribute to the team. So it was really good to put on some runs for the team in a situation like that where the game was evenly poised,” he said.

Hodge said Towhid Hridoy’s remarkable 242 not out for Bangladesh had inspired the West Indies batters to believe they could produce similar performances on a batting-friendly surface.

“Anybody who had the opportunity to witness that would have appreciated the skill and the power of such an innings, regardless of the opponent. It was just proof that the wicket is really good. I think the notion was, if he could do it, why can’t we do it? And it turned out to be the exact same thing,” he said.

Asked whether West Indies were looking to bat for a draw rather than force a result, Hodge dismissed the suggestion, saying both teams were simply trying to put themselves in the best possible position.

Looking ahead to the final day, Hodge identified spin bowling as a potentially decisive factor, admitting that Bangladesh’s spinners had already managed to extract turn from the surface.

“I think spin is going to be key. Some of the Bangladeshi guys were getting some turn, and they were able to create some quiet periods in the match. But it’s just a matter of the mindset and how the other guys approach it. Pacers, spinners, everybody has their fair share to do tomorrow,” he said.

item.title: Parliament session begins Monday, premises announced smoke-free area
item.description:
The 4th session of the 13th Jatiya Sangsad will begin tomorrow and will continue till 18 November.

The fifth meeting of the Business Advisory Committee of the 13th Jatiya Sangsad today, Sunday, decided to conclude the fourth session of parliament on 18 November, with daily sittings scheduled to begin at 4:20 pm, except on government holidays (Fridays and Saturdays).

The meeting, chaired by Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad, Bir Bikrom, MP, was held at the Cabinet Room of the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban today.

Prime Minister and Leader of the House Tarique Rahman, MP, attended the meeting along with Leader of the Opposition Md Shafiqur Rahman, MP, and other committee members.

The meeting discussed the allocation of time for parliamentary business and the duration of the fourth session of the 13th Jatiya Sangsad.

The committee also authorised the Speaker to make any necessary changes to the sitting schedule and working days of the session, said a press release of parliament secretariat.

The meeting was informed that the government had submitted one bill for consideration during the session. It was also informed that the government had promulgated three ordinances between the third and fourth sessions. These are the Public Procurement (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, and the Special Solar Power Installation Ordinance, 2026. The ordinances will be placed before parliament at the first sitting of the session.

A total of 3,751 questions have been received for the session, including 174 for the prime minister and 3,577 for other ministers.

Besides, the committee received 92 notices seeking the attention of the House under Rule 71 and 281 notices of motions under Rule 131.

During the meeting, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman proposed declaring the Jatiya Sangsad premises a smoke-free area. All members of the committee unanimously welcomed the proposal.

The prime minister also sought an update on the installation of the sound system in parliament. In response, Parliament Secretariat Secretary Barrister Md Golam Sarwar Bhuiyan informed him that the new sound system would be inaugurated at 3:30 pm tomorrow under the supervision of the Public Works Department.

Regarding the installation of solar panels on the parliament premises, Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal, who heads the relevant subcommittee, informed the meeting that the proposed system would generate seven megawatts of electricity.

He said the system would meet parliament’s electricity demand, which stands at around six megawatts during sessions and considerably less at other times, while surplus electricity would be supplied to the national grid.

The prime minister instructed the authorities concerned to ensure electricity storage facilities alongside solar power generation.

The deputy speaker also briefed the committee on the latest progress in the e-Parliament project and recruitment against vacant posts in the Jatiya Sangsad.

The meeting was attended, among others, by committee members Gayeshwar Chandra Roy, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal, Chief Whip Md Nurul Islam Moni, Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman, ATM Azharul Islam and Opposition Chief Whip Md Nahid Islam.

Parliament Secretariat Secretary Barrister Md Golam Sarwar Bhuiyan provided secretarial assistance at the meeting. Senior officials of the Parliament Secretariat were also present.

item.title: Sheikh Hasina will never be welcomed back by people: Rizvi
item.description:
Should Sheikh Hasina return to the country, the people will never accord her a reception, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, Acting Secretary-General of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and Political Adviser to the Prime Minister said on Sunday.

He also said that Sheikh Hasina is currently issuing threats from India, saying, “I am coming back, I will do this and that.” By issuing such declarations from India, she imagines she can return home to crowds greeting her with drums and applause; she is merely indulging in daydreams.

Ruhul Kabir Rizvi made these remarks as the chief guest today at a discussion organised by the Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) to mark the National Revolution and Solidarity Day on 7 November. The event took place at the Teacher-Student Centre (TSC) auditorium of Dhaka University.

Addressing the gathering, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi declared, “In Bengal—a land that gives birth to brave sons—no fugitive, no coward who flees like a jackal, and no tyrant who hesitates not to spill the blood of their own country’s children will ever fly back to usurp power with public acceptance. This will simply never happen.”

Criticising Sheikh Hasina’s regime, Rizvi noted that while her father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, had established BAKSAL, Sheikh Hasina crafted a far more terrifying incarnation of it under a different guise. During her rule, every sphere of the state was brought under her absolute control.

The BNP acting secretary-general added that the regime maintained its grip on power by weaponising state institutions, including law enforcement agencies.

Supported by the Indian government on one hand and controlling state machinery on the other, she established a fascist regime, he stated.

The July 2024 Mass Uprising was the culmination of long-standing student and public protests and resistance against this tyranny, Rizvi added.

7 November marked the beginning of multi-party democracy

Highlighting the significance of 7 November as National Revolution and Solidarity Day, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi remarked that during the 17 years of fascist rule, official observance of the day was prohibited. Nevertheless, various social and political organisations kept the occasion alive, ensuring that the essence and underlying spirit of 7 November were never erased.

He added that 7 November initiated the journey of multi-party democracy in Bangladesh and secured democratic rights. It also marked the beginning of a foreign policy and domestic decision-making process free from external influence. Who Bangladesh chooses to befriend or build alliances with remains the sole prerogative of its government and people; Bangladesh’s foreign policy will not be dictated by external instructions or signals.

Rizvi further observed that after independence, a climate was created where citizens were deprived of freedom of speech and political expression. Anyone criticising the government risked enforced disappearance or extrajudicial killing. The Rakkhi Bahini was formed to ruthlessly suppress opposition leaders and activists. The events of 7 November delivered the nation from that atmosphere, establishing an environment for fearless political expression.

Speaking at the event, Chhatra Dal Central President Rakibul Islam Rakib stated that Bangladesh failed to achieve genuine independence immediately after 1971. During that era, fascism and BAKSAL were repeatedly imposed on the nation, alongside multiple coups within the military. However, through the Sepoy-People’s Revolution and the landmark steps taken by the martyred President Ziaur Rahman, the independence and sovereignty of Bangladesh were ultimately safeguarded.

Rakib further remarked that from the establishment of BAKSAL to the consolidation of fascism up until 2024, only one political entity has been consistently responsible: the Awami League (whose activities are currently banned in the country).

The party has repeatedly posed a threat to Bangladesh’s independence and sovereignty, he stated. 

The JCD central president further said the Awami League compromised national interests in its dealings with neighbouring states and engaged in continuous conspiracies. Although its leaders have now fled the country, their plotting remains unabated.

Moderated by JCD Central General Secretary Nasir Uddin, the discussion was also addressed by its Organisational Secretary Amanullah Aman, Senior Joint General Secretary Shyamal Malum, alongside leaders and activists from city, various universities, and college units of the organisation.

item.title: Bangladesh Bank offers special facility to curb price hikes of 10 commodities ahead of Ramadan
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank (BB) has instructed banks to keep cash margin requirements at the minimum level, based on banker-customer relationships, when opening letters of credit (LCs) for importing 10 essential commodities, including edible oil, sugar, chickpeas, onions and dates, ahead of the upcoming month of Ramadan.

The central bank said the initiative was aimed at facilitating imports of essential consumer goods and keeping market prices within an affordable range. If price increases can be prevented, consumers will be able to buy these commodities at relatively resonable prices.

Bangladesh Bank issued a circular in this regard on Sunday and sent it to the managing directors and chief executive officers of all scheduled banks in the country.

The circular said the directive, issued under the authority granted by Section 45 of the Bank Company Act 1991, would come into immediate effect and remain valid until 15 March 2027.

Which commodities are covered?

The 10 commodities for which the central bank has instructed banks to keep LC margins at the minimum level are rice, wheat and flour, onions, lentils, edible oil (soybean and palm oil), sugar, chickpeas, peas, spices and dates.

Banks have also been advised to give the highest priority to opening LCs for imports of these commodities to ensure adequate and uninterrupted supplies in the domestic market.

What is an LC margin and how does it affect imports?

Simply put, an LC margin is the amount of cash or security that a trader or importer must deposit with a bank when opening a letter of credit for imports. It is generally calculated as a certain percentage of the total LC value.

For example, if the margin is 100 per cent, the importer must deposit an amount equivalent to the full value of the import to open the LC. If the margin is kept at a minimum or relaxed, an importer can open an LC by depositing a much smaller amount of cash, depending on the relationship with the bank and the available capital.

A lower cash margin requirement when opening LCs reduces pressure on traders' own capital. As a result, many importers, including small and medium-sized businesses, can import larger quantities of goods more easily. This helps increase market supplies and keep prices under control.

On the other hand, if the cash margin is set at 100 per cent or a high rate, a large amount of traders' cash remains tied up with banks. This reduces importers' ability to open LCs, potentially lowering market supplies and creating artificial shortages, with the risk of sharp price increases.

Why does demand rise during Ramadan?

Every year, demand for essential commodities such as chickpeas, lentils, edible oil, sugar, spices and dates increases several times during the holy month of Ramadan compared with normal periods.

Eating habits change during Ramadan. Iftar and sehri meals often include items such as chickpeas, peyaju (onion fritters), beguni (aubergine fritters), fruit drinks and sweets. As a result, consumption of edible oil, sugar, chickpeas, lentils and spices increases.

Large-scale iftar parties are also organised by families, corporations and various institutions during the month, creating additional pressure on wholesale and retail markets.

Consumers also tend to buy larger quantities of certain commodities at the beginning of Ramadan and store them at home. This common practice creates a temporary surge in demand in the market.

item.title: Several crude bombs explode in succession near DU’s TSC, 2 detained
item.description:
Several crude bombs exploded in succession in the area of the Teacher-Student Centre (TSC) of Dhaka University on Sunday evening.

Students and people present at the scene detained two men on suspicion of their involvement in the incident. They were later taken to Shahbagh police station.

Earlier, another cocktail bomb exploded in front of the university's Nabab Nawab Ali Chowdhury Senate Building.

Witnesses said the two men attempted to flee after detonating several cocktail bombs in the TSC area. They were detained while trying to escape through the area adjacent to the metro rail station. People present at the scene then beat them up.

It was not immediately known whether anyone had been injured in the explosions. The identities of the two detainees were also not immediately available.

item.title: Devotees observe Kartik Brata at Loknath Ashram
item.description:
Followers of Loknath Brahmachari observe a month-long fast during the Bengali calendar month Kartik, praying for the well-being of their loved ones. To mark Kartik Brata, devotees and followers of Loknath have gathered at the Shri Shri Loknath Brahmachari Ashram in Baradi, Sonargaon, Narayanganj.

Observing the ritual known as “Rakher Upobash” or “Kartik Brata”, devotees light oil lamps and incense and offer prayers on every Saturday and Tuesday during the final 15 days of the Bengali month of Kartik. Followers travel to the Baradi Ashram from different parts of the country to take part in the observance, spending their time in prayer and worship.

item.title: Consumers forced to pay Tk 300–440 extra for cooking gas
item.description:
Consumers are still unable to buy liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) at government-fixed prices, despite increases in the commissions for importers, distributors and retailers when the prices were last adjusted.

In Dhaka, consumers are having to pay at least Tk 300 extra for a 12kg cylinder in some areas, while the additional amount reaches Tk 440 in others. Prices are also higher than the official rates in markets outside the capital.

On 2 November, the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) set the price of a 12kg LPG cylinder at Tk 2,060. The 12kg cylinder is the most widely used size for household cooking.

A visit to 15 LPG shops in different parts of Dhaka on Saturday found that 12kg cylinders were selling for Tk 2,350 to Tk 2,500. Sellers were also charging an additional Tk 1,200 to Tk 1,400 for 45kg cylinders.

When the new prices were announced, the commission for importers of 12kg cylinders, covering storage and bottling costs, was increased by around Tk 82. The distributors' commission was raised from Tk 50 to Tk 85, while the retailers' commission went up from Tk 45 to Tk 70. However, distributors and retailers claim that these commissions are insufficient to cover their costs.

On the issue of higher prices, two major LPG importing companies say they have increased supplies and that action should be taken against those charging consumers extra. Distributors, on the other hand, allege that there is a supply shortage and that some companies are also charging higher prices.

BERC Chairman Jalal Ahmed told Prothom Alo that the commission had received complaints about sales at higher prices and was working on the issue. It was also examining the extent to which LPG consumption in the industrial sector had increased.

"Two members of the commission are visiting the field. Those who buy LPG from other suppliers instead of importing it themselves are mainly responsible for selling it at higher prices. BERC is also looking into this," he said.

With gas connections unavailable and LPG prices high, a household in Dhanmondi has turned to a traditional wood-burning stove for cooking.

More than 10 million consumers use LPG in Bangladesh. Around 80 per cent of the fuel is used for household cooking. Demand for LPG began rising sharply in 2015 after new household gas connections were suspended. Annual LPG demand in the country now exceeds 1.8 million tonnes.

Nearly 99 per cent of the sector is controlled by private operators, who import and distribute the fuel. The remaining 1 per cent is produced and supplied domestically by a state-owned company.

According to the LPG Operators Association of Bangladesh (LOAB), the organisation representing LPG importers, and BERC sources, the country imported 158,000 tonnes of LPG in August, 156,000 tonnes in September and less than 142,000 tonnes in October. However, another 40,200 tonnes arrived in the country by 4 November. LOAB has repeatedly warned distributors against selling LPG at prices above the official rates.

Abu Sayeed Raza, chief marketing officer of Meghna Fresh LPG, told Prothom Alo that the company was supplying LPG at maximum capacity from its four plants. It was also supplying companies that were unable to import the fuel themselves. Therefore, LPG supplies in the market should remain normal. Market surveillance by law enforcement agencies should be strengthened.

Some importers say there is a shortage of LPG in the global market. Supplies from the Middle East have almost come to a halt, while only negligible quantities are available from African countries. Most of Bangladesh's LPG imports are now coming from the United States, where importers have to pay higher prices. Shipping costs for bringing LNG from the United States have also increased. Moreover, Bangladesh lacks sufficient infrastructure to store large quantities of LPG. Importers also risk incurring substantial losses if they build up stocks and the conflict in the Middle East ends, causing international prices to fall.

Azam J Chowdhury, former president of LOAB, told Prothom Alo that ensuring LPG supplies had become more important than prices amid the prevailing global situation.

"Even though we are importing LPG at higher prices, we are supplying it at the rates fixed by BERC. If LPG prices increase, consumer numbers will fall, which is not what operators want. However, anyone is selling LPG at whatever price they wish in shops across the country. Proper monitoring is necessary to prevent this," he said.

According to the LPG Gas Traders Cooperative Society, BERC has not extended the same benefits to distributors and retailers as it has to importers. The increase in commissions has also fallen short of their requirements.

The society said market supplies had yet to improve. Trucks had to wait for long periods at company plants to collect LPG, adding to their costs. Some companies were also charging higher prices.

Abu Taher Qureshi, treasurer of the society, told Prothom Alo that distributors could supply LPG at the commissions set by BERC outside Dhaka, but doing so in the capital was simply not feasible because of high transportation costs.

Distributors are therefore unable to sell at the officially fixed prices, he said.

The Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection is also aware that cylinder gas is being sold above government-fixed prices.

Its Director General Md Zahirul Islam told Prothom Alo, "We are receiving reports of higher prices. In many cases, sellers keep the gas hidden and sell it discreetly. We have already conducted drives in different areas and fined some businesses. We conducted another drive last Thursday, and these operations will continue tomorrow as well."

Higher prices across Dhaka

Visits to eight retail shops and four dealer outlets in Shewrapara in Mirpur and Sector 12 of Uttara found that 12kg cylinders were selling for Tk 2,350 to Tk 2,500 at all the outlets.

However, most sellers were reluctant to sell gas to anyone other than familiar customers. They feared that the prospective buyers might be journalists or officials from the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection. When customers approached them, they often claimed that no gas was available.

When this correspondent tried to buy gas from a shopkeeper named Md Sayem in Mirpur's 60 Feet area, he initially said there was no gas and that it would be available in two days.

The correspondent later collected his phone number and called him two hours later to enquire about supplies. The seller first asked about the caller's identity. After verifying the caller's name, identity and home address, he confirmed that gas was available. However, he quoted a price of Tk 2,500.

At a shop in Uttara Sector 12, a retailer named Asadullah Noor was found selling 12kg cylinders for Tk 2,400. He claimed that he had bought each cylinder for Tk 2,250.

Prices also high in rural areas

Prothom Alo correspondents collected price information from markets in five upazilas outside Dhaka on Saturday. They found that LPG cylinders were selling for Tk 40 to Tk 240 above the government-fixed price.

In Sitakunda of Chattogram, 12kg LPG cylinders were selling for Tk 2,100 to Tk 2,400. In Bagmara of Rajshahi, prices ranged from Tk 2,200 to Tk 2,300, while in Bauphal of Patuakhali they were selling for Tk 2,100 to Tk 2,200. In different shops in Sakhipur of Tangail, some sellers were charging Tk 2,200 and others Tk 2,300.

Jahangir Talukder, owner of Jahangir Enterprise, a dealer in Sakhipur, told Prothom Alo that companies were unable to supply gas according to demand. His business had not received any gas from the company so far this month, resulting in a temporary shortage in the market.

In various markets in Dharmapasha upazila of Sunamganj, including Badshaganj, Gachhtala, Dharmapasha and Joyshree, 12kg cylinders were selling for Tk 2,100 to Tk 2,200.

Rafiqul Islam of Haji Traders, a distributor at Dharmapasha East Market in the upazila headquarters, said they were supplying cylinders to retailers in all markets across the upazila at Tk 2,020 to Tk 2,030.

Among neighbouring countries, Bangladesh has the highest LPG prices. Prothom Alo published a report on the issue on 7 October, which found that LPG prices in Bangladesh were more than twice those in Kolkata, India.

However, India sells LPG through state-owned agencies and also provides subsidies. LPG prices in Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka are also lower than in Bangladesh.

The Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (BPC) received government approval to import LPG in January, but it has yet to import any.

M Shamsul Alam, energy adviser to the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), told Prothom Alo that BERC had rushed to set higher prices, effectively facilitating business interests. On top of that, billions of taka are being extracted from consumers by selling LPG at even higher prices. Yet the state remains silent, and there is no remedy within the energy sector's administration. This raises questions about the image of a democratic government.

[Prothom Alo correspondents in Sitakunda, Bagmara, Bauphal, Sakhipur and Dharmapasha contributed to this report.]

item.title: HSC supplementary exam: Will the results count towards university admission?
item.description:
Supplementary examinations will be held on 1 December for candidates who failed in up to two subjects (excluding the fourth subject) in this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations. The aim is to increase their opportunities to enter higher education. However, questions have arisen over whether the initiative will achieve its intended purpose.

The reason is that the preliminary application period for first-year undergraduate admission in the 2026–27 academic session at Dhaka University and Rajshahi University will end this month. Applications will also open this month at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) and Jagannath University. Other universities are also beginning their admission processes.

In other words, the lack of coordination between the supplementary examination schedule and the universities’ admission processes threatens to undermine the very purpose of holding the examinations at short notice.

Education experts say that coordination was needed when scheduling the supplementary examinations and the university admission process. If an integrated timeline had been set, students would have reaped the benefits of this initiative. Due to a lack of coordination, students now risk suffering as a result on the one hand, whilst on the other, the positive decision to hold the exams within a month has also come into question.

This year, a total of 422,905 candidates failed in one or two subjects. Among them, 298,040 candidates failed in one subject, whilst 124,865 failed in two subjects.

A source in the education division stated that although discussions took place on this matter among the University Grants Commission (UGC), the education boards, and the universities, students may not reap the benefits of this initiative this time due to a lack of interest from top-tier universities. However, opportunities for admission will remain open in several other institutions.

An official from the Dhaka Education Board told Prothom Alo that this year, for the first time, supplementary examinations are being held within a month of the results being published. As a result, there may be some shortcomings. However, he believes that from next year onwards, this facility will be available across all universities, and other discrepancies will be resolved.

Not only that, complications may also arise regarding the timing of the release of results for answer script re-scrutiny and re-evaluation. For instance, a candidate who failed in three subjects may have applied for re-scrutiny. If they subsequently pass in one or two subjects as a result of the re-scrutiny, they would become eligible to sit the supplementary exam.

HSC: Re-evaluation sought for over 1 million scripts, deadline extended

However, according to the announcement by the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee, the re-scrutiny results will be published on 23 November, whereas the ongoing deadline for filling out the supplementary exam forms is 9 November.

Consequently, the deadline for form submission will expire before the re-scrutiny results are published. As a result, even if some candidates become eligible to take the supplementary exam due to a change in their results, they may still miss out on the opportunity.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, a resident of Chattogram told Prothom Alo that several children of a neighbour had failed in two or three subjects in this year's HSC examinations, and some of them have applied for result re-scrutiny. Now, if the re-scrutiny results show that they have passed in one or two out of the three subjects, they will become eligible for the supplementary exam.

However, questions have been raised over how they will participate in the exam if the re-scrutiny results are published after the deadline for form submission has passed. The matter ought to be taken into consideration by the government.

When asked, Professor Jasmin Taslima Banu, Controller of Examinations at the Dhaka Education Board, told Prothom Alo that all necessary measures would be taken in the best interests of the students.

The results of the HSC and equivalent examinations were published on 31 October. This year, out of 1,240,798 candidates across 11 education boards, 646,685 passed, representing an average pass rate of 52.12 per cent. A total of 40,084 students achieved a GPA-5. This year, a total of 422,905 candidates failed in one or two subjects. Among them, 298,040 candidates failed in one subject, whilst 124,865 failed in two subjects.

The supplementary examinations will begin on 1 December. Both regular and irregular candidates will be eligible to sit them. Form submission began on 5 November and will continue until 9 November. The deadline for payment of fees is 10 November.

Arrangement of supplementary examinations

Usually, if a candidate fails in one or more subjects in public examinations such as the SSC and HSC, they have to sit the examinations again the following year. In that case, they can choose to take the examinations only in the subjects they failed or, if they wish, in all subjects.

However, students who fail in just one or two subjects have to wait an entire year to retake the examinations. Taking this problem into consideration, the authorities have decided to hold examinations within a month of the publication of results for candidates who failed in up to two subjects this year.

The supplementary examinations will begin on 1 December. Both regular and irregular candidates will be eligible to sit them. Form submission began on 5 November and will continue until 9 November. The deadline for payment of fees is 10 November. The form submission fee has been set at Tk 125 for each theoretical paper or subject and Tk 25 for each practical paper or subject. In addition, the examination centre fee is Tk 450.

Meanwhile, the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee has instructed educational institutions not to charge candidates any additional fees in the name of examination form submission. A notice issued on 5 November said legal action would be taken against the head of any institution and the institution itself if the instruction was violated.

HSC result 2026: Worst performance in 22 years

University admission process begins

Online applications for first-year undergraduate admission at Dhaka University for the 2026–27 academic session will open on 11 November. The application period will continue until 25 November.

Admission tests will be held in five units. The Science Unit test will take place on 12 December, the Arts, Law and Social Sciences Unit test on 19 December, the Fine Arts Unit test (general knowledge and drawing) on 22 December, the Business Studies Unit test on 26 December, and the IBA Unit test on 5 December.

When asked about the matter, Dhaka University Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Academic) Professor Abdus Salam told Prothom Alo that the decision to hold supplementary examinations for candidates who failed in up to two subjects in the HSC and equivalent examinations was a positive initiative. It had given them an opportunity to pass, he said.

Referring to the level of competition in Dhaka University's admission tests, the pro-VC said that previously around 80 candidates competed for each university seat. The figure now stood at between 60 and 70. Even so, 95 to 96 per cent of those who sit the admission tests fail to obtain the pass mark.

Drawing on his own experience, Professor Abdus Salam said that even if students who passed the supplementary examinations were allowed to sit Dhaka University's admission tests, he did not think they would benefit that much.

Meanwhile, preliminary applications for admission to the undergraduate (honours) programmes at Rajshahi University for the same academic session will open on 12 November and close on 27 November. The admission tests for the ‘B’, ‘C’ and ‘A’ units at the university will be held on 8, 9 and 16 January, respectively.

Professor Abdus Salam, pro-VC (academic), University of DhakaThe decision to hold supplementary examinations for candidates who failed in up to two subjects in the HSC and equivalent examinations was a positive initiative. It had given them an opportunity to pass.

The admission test for Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) will be held on 16 January. Professor Kamrul Hasan, head of BUET’s admission test committee, told Prothom Alo that the date for opening applications had not yet been approved at a meeting of the Academic Council.

However, he expected the process to begin shortly after the 20th this month. He said they always waited for the publication of the re-scrutiny results before proceeding, and would do the same this year.

Professor Kamrul Hasan’s comments suggested that candidates who pass the supplementary examinations would not be allowed to sit BUET’s admission test. He said only a small number of students were given the opportunity to take the admission test at BUET. “What would be the point of allowing candidates who pass the supplementary examinations to sit the admission test?” he asked.

Online applications for admission to the first-year undergraduate (honours) and Bachelor of Business Administration (BBA) programmes at Jagannath University for the 2026–27 academic session will open on 15 November and continue until 10 December.

HSC results: Fewer pass, over 800,000 seats in higher education to remain vacant

This means the application periods for Dhaka University and Rajshahi University will end before the supplementary examination results are published. Although admission tests at these universities will take place later, there will be no opportunity to consider supplementary examination results when determining candidates’ eligibility to apply. Similar complications may arise when other universities begin their admission processes.

According to UGC data, there are around 1,492,000 seats in higher education this year. More than one million of these are at public universities and affiliated institutions, while private universities have more than 400,000 seats. This means that even if all students who passed this year enrol in higher education, more than 845,000 seats are expected to remain vacant.

In this situation, people concerned believe it is essential to coordinate university admission schedules alongside the initiative to hold supplementary examinations to expand access to higher education.

They say the necessary arrangements should be made to ensure that students who pass the supplementary examinations, as well as those who pass following re-scrutiny of their results, can take part in the admission race. Otherwise, despite the initiative to hold the examinations quickly, a large number of students may be deprived of a crucial opportunity to enter higher education.

According to UGC data, there are around 1,492,000 seats in higher education this year. More than one million of these are at public universities and affiliated institutions, while private universities have more than 400,000 seats. This means that even if all students who passed this year enrol in higher education, more than 845,000 seats are expected to remain vacant.

When asked about the matter, Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee President and Dhaka Education Board Chairman Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman told Prothom Alo that the entire situation had to be taken into consideration. It was the government’s goodwill that had made it possible, for the first time, for HSC candidates who failed in up to two subjects to retake the examinations within a month of the publication of results, he said.

At the same time, they also had to keep the issue of session backlogs at universities in mind. However, even if a few universities do not provide this opportunity this time, there are many other universities and colleges available. It is hoped that candidates who pass the supplementary examinations will be able to take advantage of admission opportunities at those institutions, he added.

item.title: Enovar marks first anniversary with 700 dealers and over 400 products
item.description:
Enovar, the flagship brand of Bangladesh’s leading industrial conglomerate AKIJ Resource, has completed its first year of operations.

Launched in 2025 with electrical products, the brand has expanded its portfolio to more than 400 products across electrical, home appliances, pumps and tools categories within just one year.

During this time, it has established a network of 700 dealers across the country, strengthening its market presence and distribution capabilities, reports a press release.

To mark the first anniversary, a program was held on Sunday (8 November) at AKIJ House in Tejgaon, Dhaka. Sheikh Jasim Uddin, managing director of AKIJ Resource, attended the event as the chief guest

Addressing the event, Sheikh Jasim Uddin said, “Enovar’s one-year journey marks an important milestone for us. Within a short period, we have been able to earn the trust of customers and business partners through product quality and new innovation. Keeping our partners in mind, we are focusing on developing products that meet evolving preferences. To achieve this, we are using advanced technology, robotic arms and fully automated systems in our factories.”

He further said, “We believe that the combination of modern technology, quality products, and reliable services will make everyday life easier and more comfortable for people. We aspire to make Enovar’s products available to consumers in every corner of the country.”

Masud Al Amin Rajib, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of AKIJ Light Engineering Limited said, “Enovar’s first year has been a journey of progress, opportunities and significant milestones for us. Our goal is to deliver products that meet customers’ everyday needs through a combination of modern design, technology, quality and reliability. Building a portfolio of more than 400 products and establishing a network of 700 dealers nationwide within such a short period have further strengthened the foundation for our future growth.”

He added, “Our goal is not limited to only selling products; we are equally committed to ensuring after-sales service. We have a skilled service team that provides support to consumers based on their needs across the country. Our aim is to establish Enovar as a trusted brand by earning customer confidence, ensuring product availability and delivering quality customer service.”

Md Afsar Uddin, chief people officer of AKIJ Resource, Mohammad Towfique Hasan, chief business development officer, Sohanur Rahman Sohan, deputy chief operating officer, Md Golam Kibria Sarkar, chief financial officer of AKIJ Light Engineering Limited, Mohammad Sajjadul Islam, head of marketing, Md Touhidul Islam Faisal, head of operation, along with officials from various business units of AKIJ Resource, attended the event.

Inspired by its founding philosophy “Designed for Now” Enovar’s current product portfolio includes switches, sockets, LED lights, electric cookers, gas stoves, rice cookers, geysers, water pumps, hardware, and power tools, among others.

From home construction and electrical installations to kitchen and everyday household needs, the brand continues to diversify and expand its product range to meet evolving consumer demands.

item.title: West Indies take 315-run lead, Bangladesh face record chase
item.description:
CRICKET-BAN-WIS-TEST

It was a frustrating day for Bangladesh as the West Indies strengthened their grip on the Sylhet Test, piling up 338 runs in 79 overs on the fourth day, Sunday, to take their overall lead to 315 runs.

The visitors reached 345 for three in their second innings at stumps, with centurion Kavem Hodge unbeaten on 140 and Amir Jangoo on 20.

Bangladesh now face a daunting task in the final innings, as they will need to break their record for the highest successful run chase in Test cricket to win the match.

Bangladesh's highest successful fourth-innings chase came against the West Indies in 2009, when they scored 215 to secure victory. They have never successfully chased down a target of more than 200 runs in a Test since.

Hodge brings up third Test century

Kavem Hodge brought up his third Test century with a sweep off Taijul Islam's bowling, collecting a delivery outside leg stump and guiding it to the boundary.

The right-hander remained unbeaten on 140 at the close, anchoring the West Indies' second-innings effort.

Bangladesh face a record chase

Bangladesh's highest successful run chase in Test cricket remains the 215-run target they overhauled against the West Indies in 2009.

With the visitors already 315 runs ahead in the ongoing Sylhet Test, Bangladesh will need to produce their greatest fourth-innings performance to secure victory.

Wickham joins an exclusive club

Kevin Wickham became only the eighth West Indies cricketer to score two half-centuries on his Test debut.

Brief scores

West Indies: 356 and 345/3 (Kevon Hodge 140*, Kevin Wickham 78, Brandon King 61; Taijul Islam 2/118, Mehidy Hasan Miraz 1/58).

Bangladesh: 386 (Towhid Hridoy 242*, Mushfiqur Rahim 34; Jomel Warrican 4/104).

West Indies lead by 315 runs.

item.title: Why are foreign banks moving away from Bangladesh?
item.description:
The decisions by Standard Chartered and HSBC to wind down their retail banking operations in Bangladesh have raised several questions. Does this signal a crisis of confidence among international banks in the Bangladeshi market, or does it reflect a shift in global banking strategies? Mamun Rashid examines the issue.

At one time, the presence of international banks in Bangladesh’s banking sector was regarded as a symbol of professionalism, modern technology, superior customer service and good governance. Over the years, several generations of customers have developed relationships of trust and confidence with institutions such as Standard Chartered and HSBC.

It is therefore only natural that Standard Chartered Bank’s decision to sell its retail banking business in Bangladesh, following HSBC’s earlier announcement that it would wind down its retail banking operations, has raised questions: Are international banks losing confidence in the Bangladeshi market, or is the international banking business model itself undergoing a fundamental transformation?

To find answers to these questions, we need to examine global banking strategies, competition in the local market and the economics of operating costs.

First, one point needs to be made clear: withdrawing from retail banking does not necessarily mean leaving Bangladesh altogether. Retail banking includes services such as deposits from individual customers, credit cards, home loans, personal loans, payment services and wealth management.

Corporate banking, international trade finance, treasury operations and institutional banking, on the other hand, are separate business segments. In many cases, international banks are scaling back their retail banking operations while placing greater emphasis on these other areas of business.

One of the most important reasons behind this shift is the economics of banking operations. A multinational bank has to bear more than just the costs of running branches and providing customer services. It must also make substantial investments in global technology infrastructure, cybersecurity, anti-money laundering measures, international sanctions screening, risk management, capital preservation and group-level oversight.

A significant portion of these costs does not decline even when the number of customers falls. Consequently, unless a bank has a sufficiently large customer base, deposit portfolio, loan book and transaction volume in a particular country, its operating costs per customer tend to rise.

Standard Chartered Bank wants to wind down its retail and card business in Bangladesh

Profitability is not the only consideration in a bank’s business decisions; the return generated on invested capital is equally important. If a bank invests substantial amounts of money in operating retail banking in a particular country but earns relatively modest profits, it will naturally consider alternative opportunities if the same capital could generate higher returns in another market or in corporate banking. In other words, the efficient allocation of capital has now become one of the key considerations in the business strategies of international banks.

In Bangladesh, domestic banks have extensive branch networks, long-standing customer relationships and a deep understanding of the needs of local businesses and consumers. At the same time, the expansion of mobile financial services, internet banking and digital payments has transformed the way banking services are delivered to customers.

At one time, international banks enjoyed a significant competitive advantage in credit cards, technology, international transactions and customer service. Over time, however, domestic banks have also increased their investments in these areas. As a result, much of the competitive advantage once enjoyed by foreign banks has diminished. Nevertheless, the expansion of digital services does not necessarily mean that all domestic banks are now capable of providing services that meet international standards.

Bangladesh’s banking sector is currently grappling with problems such as non-performing loans, capital shortfalls, weak corporate governance, irregularities and a crisis of depositor confidence

Such business restructuring is by no means confined to Bangladesh. Around the world, major banks are increasingly seeking to concentrate their capital in markets and business segments where they can generate relatively higher profits and better returns on investment. India offers an important example in this regard. In 2023, Citibank N.A. sold its consumer banking business in India to Axis Bank.

Standard Chartered has also sold its personal loan portfolio to Kotak Mahindra Bank and, in 2026, entered into an agreement to transfer a large portfolio of credit card customers to Federal Bank. However, the bank is also pursuing a strategy of maintaining relationships with high-net-worth customers.

There are similar precedents in Pakistan, where the local operations of RBS, Barclays and HSBC have been transferred to various domestic banks. These experiences demonstrate that when strong local banks develop the necessary capabilities, opportunities emerge for them to acquire businesses relinquished by international banks.

HSBC’s decision in Bangladesh should also be viewed as part of its broader global reassessment. The bank has decided to restructure its retail banking operations in several markets, including Australia, Indonesia and Sri Lanka. Therefore, global strategy, capital management and profitability considerations have played important roles in its decision to scale back operations in Bangladesh. At the same time, the country's own market conditions cannot be ignored.

Bangladesh’s banking sector is currently grappling with problems such as non-performing loans, capital shortfalls, weak corporate governance, irregularities and a crisis of depositor confidence. Politically influenced lending, loans to related parties and the failure to take effective action against major loan defaulters have further exposed the sector’s institutional weaknesses. According to data published by Bangladesh Bank, by the middle of 2026, nearly one-third of the country's total banking sector loans had become non-performing. The World Bank has also highlighted capital weaknesses in the country's banking system.

In such circumstances, the withdrawal of two prominent international banks from retail banking could create negative perceptions among investors and customers. However, it would be inaccurate to interpret these decisions as evidence of a complete loss of international confidence in Bangladesh's economy or banking sector. Withdrawing from retail banking and completely exiting a country are two different things.

If international banks continue their corporate banking, trade finance and institutional banking operations, their long-term business interest in Bangladesh cannot be dismissed. The real question, rather, is how Bangladesh can ensure a business and regulatory environment that sustains international banks' interest in investing in the country.

The transfer of foreign banks' retail banking businesses to domestic banks could also create new opportunities. An acquiring bank can gain access to deposits, credit card customers, skilled employees and an established customer base all at once. This reduces the time and investment required to develop a new market from scratch.

However, acquiring a large portfolio does not automatically guarantee success. Such transactions also involve significant challenges, including assessing loan quality, retaining customers, integrating technology systems, ensuring cybersecurity and protecting customers' personal information. Bangladesh Bank must therefore ensure proper valuation of the businesses, assess the financial capacity of acquiring institutions and safeguard the interests of both customers and employees.

The key challenge facing Bangladesh’s banking sector today is to restore institutional credibility. This requires appointing qualified and competent individuals to bank boards, ensuring transparency in lending, controlling related-party lending, taking effective measures to recover non-performing loans, and ensuring independent and rigorous oversight by the regulatory authorities. Domestic banks must not limit themselves to competing over branch expansion or customer acquisition. They must also ensure efficient capital allocation, sound risk management, technological capabilities and compliance with international standards.

The withdrawal of international banks from retail banking should therefore not be viewed from a single perspective. While it reflects a shift in global banking strategies, it also presents an opportunity for domestic banks in Bangladesh to demonstrate their capabilities. However, acquiring the customers or business portfolios of foreign banks is relatively easy. The real challenge lies in retaining those customers’ trust and ensuring that they continue to receive services that meet international standards.

item.title: Finance minister, state minister find discrepancies in GDP figures
item.description:
Several discrepancies have been found in the calculation of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) during the previous government’s tenure. A committee identified the inconsistencies through a forensic audit. The report will be published soon after being reviewed by experts.

Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury and State Minister for Planning Md Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki made the remarks at a discussion held at the auditorium of the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) in Agargaon, Dhaka, on Sunday, marking National Statistics Day.

Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury was the chief guest at the event. Other special guests included the Prime Minister’s Political Adviser Zahir Uddin Swapan, Adviser to the Finance and Planning Ministry Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, and State Minister Md Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki.

The event was chaired by Md Firoz Sarkar, secretary of the Statistics and Informatics Division. BBS Director General Md Shamimul Haque delivered the welcome address.

BBS Director Kabir Uddin Ahmad, Dhaka University professor Syed Shahadat Hossain and Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) Director General AK Enamul Haque also spoke at the meeting.

Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury said no meaningful work could be done using questionable statistics. Doing so was tantamount to deceiving oneself. Information was the government's most important asset. The government was therefore granting full independence to the BBS and was also considering its staff shortages.

The finance minister further said the forensic audit had been conducted to investigate past irregularities in depth, not to target anyone. The more information was made publicly available, the more errors and inconsistencies would come to light, creating opportunities for corrections.

The importance of data and digital infrastructure was increasing further in the age of artificial intelligence, he added.

Prime Minister's Political Adviser Zahir Uddin Swapan said scientifically generated data carried considerable weight. Accurate statistics could play an important role in the country's development planning and policymaking.

Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, adviser to the Finance and Planning Ministry, said an attempt had been made during the previous government's tenure to construct a particular narrative using statistics.

Reviews of past data had revealed inconsistencies in various areas, including GDP calculations, he stated.

According to him, there were also widespread discrepancies in social safety net programme data. Many of those who were supposed to receive assistance had been left out, he said.

Titumir said the number of water vessels in the country had previously been reported at 13,000. However, a review found that the actual figure was 267,000. Initiatives were being taken to introduce digital register exchanges to address such discrepancies. He added that a kind of hybrid war involving misinformation was currently underway.

State Minister Md Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki said it was impossible to understand where the country stood, where it wanted to go or where things were going wrong without accurate information. The government had therefore taken initiatives to restore public confidence in statistics.

He said a forensic audit had been conducted on statistics compiled during the previous government. The review found significant discrepancies in the GDP figures that had earlier been questioned. Evidence of these inconsistencies had also been found.

The state minister further said the BBS was now publishing various statistics, including the Consumer Price Index (CPI), on its own, without requiring the minister's signature.

item.title: Why is GenZ looking abroad?
item.description:
Graduation is over, but does that really mean the end of one chapter? Or is it the beginning of another struggle? Morning classes, catching up with friends in between, returning home for a comforting lunch prepared by your mother, followed by an afternoon nap. Life changes in the blink of an eye during the final year of university. Jobs, interviews and CVs — it suddenly feels like an attempt to grow up overnight. And now, another concern has entered the picture: moving abroad.

An increasing number of young people from Generation Z are looking overseas. The figures reflect this growing trend. According to UNESCO, around 52,800 Bangladeshi students were pursuing higher education abroad in 2023, compared with just over 24,000 in 2013. The number has more than doubled in a decade. But what is driving this trend? Why has abroad become the preferred destination for so many members of Gen Z?

Gruelling competition for university places

Before discussing the decision to move abroad after graduation, it is worth considering those who make the choice at the very first stage of higher education. For many students, the decision to leave the country after completing their HSC (Higher Secondary Education) examinations stems from a range of factors. The biggest, however, is the gruelling competition for admission to universities at home.

On average, 36 candidates compete for every available place at public universities. A similar level of competition is gradually becoming evident at private universities as well. Such intense pressure is fostering a negative attitude among students towards building their futures in Bangladesh.

Tasmim Binte Karim Omi is currently living in St John's, Canada. She left Bangladesh four years ago, immediately after completing her higher secondary education, to pursue higher studies abroad. Her experience reflects much the same reality. The fear of losing the admission battle was overwhelming. That was what led her to choose overseas education. But the journey was by no means easy.

Better-quality education

After completing their undergraduate degrees, students in Bangladesh generally have three options: first, sitting for the Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examinations; second, competing for jobs at reputable private-sector organisations; and third, moving abroad in pursuit of a better life. The first two options involve competing against hundreds of thousands of applicants. For many, going abroad therefore appears to be the only alternative. It is this path that offers students at least a glimmer of hope.

In response, Jannatul says, “Access to better-quality education is the primary reason. In Bangladesh, my subject is offered at only three universities. So you can understand why, whether I want to or not, I have to give priority to countries such as those in Europe and America in search of better opportunities.”

I spoke to Jannatul Ferdous Tripti, a final-year student in the Department of Criminology and Police Science at Chittagong University. As she approaches the completion of her undergraduate studies, thoughts about the future seem to occupy much of her mind. A significant part of that anxiety concerns employment, alongside the prospect of pursuing higher education abroad.

IELTS, statements of purpose (SOPs), bank statements and sponsors' documents — the list of requirements seems endless. Despite all the complications, why does she still consider going abroad her first choice?

In response, Jannatul says, “Access to better-quality education is the primary reason. In Bangladesh, my subject is offered at only three universities. So you can understand why, whether I want to or not, I have to give priority to countries such as those in Europe and America in search of better opportunities.”

Uncertain job market

However, better-quality education is not the only reason young people are leaving the country. Uncertainty in the job market is another major factor.

According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics' Labour Force Survey 2024, the number of unemployed people in the country stood at 2.46 million in 2023. By December 2024, it had risen to approximately 2.62 million. According to the September 2026 issue of the IMF's Finance & Development magazine, nearly 36 per cent of Bangladesh's educated labour force aged 15–24, with post-secondary education, are unemployed.

Female students appear to be somewhat more inclined towards choosing overseas destinations. Behind this preference lie the desire for personal freedom, social security and the ability to become financially independent.

Given the state of the job market, is it not understandable that young people would rather seek opportunities abroad?

According to Bangladesh Bank data, students remitted more than $660 million for overseas education in the 2024–25 financial year. Faced with such a substantial investment, members of Gen Z increasingly regard foreign destinations as safer bets than staying in Bangladesh. At the heart of this preference is their desire for greater certainty in employment and their future prospects.

Reality on the other side

Let us return to Tasmim's story. She left Bangladesh four years ago and has spent all this time away from her family. She has not had an opportunity to visit home even once. Yet, in many ways, she has achieved what she had hoped to gain by leaving the country. She has found personal freedom, better education and an improved standard of living.

But there are also many things she has had to give up.

When asked what she considered the biggest challenge of living abroad, her answer was immediate: having to deal with every situation on her own.

“The challenges of living abroad are not the same for everyone. Much depends on the kind of environment in which a person has grown up. I grew up surrounded by many people, so my biggest challenge after coming to Canada was not finding people with whom I could connect and socialise in the way I wanted,” she says.

Among the thousands of Gen Z young people dreaming of moving abroad, there are also those with a different outlook. One such student told me that he had no desire to leave Bangladesh.

Although life abroad may appear colourful from a distance, such feelings are quite common among students living overseas. There is also the added pressure of establishing oneself in a new country. Yet, despite all these challenges, going abroad continues to represent a ray of hope.

Growing interest among female students

Female students appear to be somewhat more inclined towards choosing overseas destinations. Behind this preference lie the desire for personal freedom, social security and the ability to become financially independent.

Faced with lewd remarks and unwanted stares on the streets, unsafe public transport and pressure to marry at an early age, many women are looking abroad for a better quality of life.

Global statistics appear to support this trend. A German study conducted in 2021 found a notable gender gap in the desire to study abroad among first-semester university students. Of the 5,408 students surveyed, 25 per cent of female students expressed a clear intention to pursue higher education overseas. Among male students, the figure was 20 per cent.

There are different stories, too

Among the thousands of Gen Z young people dreaming of moving abroad, there are also those with a different outlook. One such student told me that he had no desire to leave Bangladesh.

His reason was simple: the prospect of living alone in a foreign country.

He says, “The environment we have grown up in since childhood in Bangladesh is completely different from what we find abroad. Even the idea of socialising is quite different there. Having grown up amid so much noise, excitement and social interaction, I find the prospect of living alone abroad rather difficult. With enough determination and courage, it is possible to do well in Bangladesh, too.”

Opportunities come with complications

There is hope, but the journey is far from straightforward. A required IELTS score, an admission letter, bank statements, sponsors' documents and, finally, a visa interview — every stage involves waiting, while the final step carries the risk of rejection. Country-specific restrictions add to the complications.

Canada has set aside only 155,000 places for new international students in 2026. Meanwhile, rising costs and growing complications in the United States and Canada have prompted many students to consider destinations in Asia and Europe.

Countries such as Germany, Italy, Finland, South Korea and China are now featuring prominently on their lists of preferred destinations. This year, 51 Bangladeshi students enrolled at Japan's Saga University, making them the largest group of international students at the institution for the first time.

Meanwhile, the number of students learning different foreign languages in Dhaka is also rising rapidly. In other words, although the destinations may be changing, the desire to go abroad remains undiminished.

Not just for education, but for livelihoods, too

According to a report by the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit (RMMRU), a total of 1,130,757 workers went abroad in 2025. A portion of them belong to Generation Z.

The acute shortage of employment opportunities at home is pushing young Bangladeshis towards the Middle East, the Far East, Europe and America in search of work.

Migrant workers are one of the principal sources of remittances for Bangladesh. Reports of people dying while attempting to reach Europe across the Mediterranean Sea or crossing borders hidden inside covered vans leave us deeply saddened.

Just as members of Gen Z leave behind the familiarity of home in pursuit of higher education, a substantial number are also willing to risk their lives in search of employment abroad.

Bangladesh remains in their hearts

For Generation Z, foreign countries have increasingly become the destination of choice. Yet many young people also want to return and work for their country. Others hope to contribute to Bangladesh while pursuing their goals from wherever they are.

Many members of this new generation have expressed such aspirations.

* Zahin Jaimah Kabir is a student of Economics at BRAC University
