This raises serious concerns that the objective was to prevent images of police operations from reaching the public.”
Several journalists, who were covering the protests, also highlighted on social media that the police was asking for government accredited press cards and not recognising cards issued by independent organizations.
“ This raises fundamental concerns, press freedom cannot be conditional on government approval, and accreditation requirements must never become a tool for excluding independent or critical voices. The right to report does not depend on whether a journalist works for an established newspaper, an independent online outlet or a digital platform. All journalists must receive equal protection, regardless of their employer and professional status,” RSF said.
In Bangladesh, IFJ documented an expansion of gatekeeping intended to restrict the media’s ability to report. The Press Information Department had revoked the accreditation of around 167 journalists between October 29, 2024 and November 7, 2024.
These measures often lead to self-censorship .
The United Nations’ Human Rights Committee, in 2020 , adopted general comment number 37 that noted that the right to peaceful assembly should be recognized. It also highlighted the obligations of state parties regarding the same.
It said that law enforcement officials must respect and ensure the exercise of fundamental rights of organisers and participants, while also protecting journalists, observers, and others from harm.
The committee further said, “The role of journalists, human rights defenders, election monitors and others involved in monitoring or reporting on assemblies is of particular importance for the full enjoyment of the right of peaceful assembly.” It added that journalists and participants have the right to record law enforcement officials.
Majumder emphasised that every journalist has an equal right to report on public events without intimidation, obstruction, or discrimination. “The police must not decide who gets to do their job based on which media organisation they represent or what their reporting might reveal. Press freedom means protecting the right of all journalists to report, including those whose coverage may be critical of the authorities,” he said.
With respect to what happened in India, RSF recommended that courts should provide effective and timely remedies when journalists’ rights are violated, and newsrooms should strengthen safety protocols. It also said that the police must put an end to physical assaults, intimidation and the confiscation of journalistic equipment.
“Let us do our jobs. We don’t want any special or VIP treatment. We already go through a lot when we are on the ground…If the fourth pillar of democracy, which is journalism, is weakened, then what will happen to democracy?” said Mishra.
Abhishek is the associate editor at Asian Dispatch. Previously, he worked as the senior correspondent, fact-check for The Quint. The story was originally published by Asian Dispatch on October 22, 2026, and has been republished by Dhaka Tribune with permission.

item.title: Why Kali wears a garland of heads, stands on Shiva
item.description:
Her skin is dark, her hair flows freely, and a garland of severed heads hangs around her neck. She carries a sword and a severed head in her hands, while Lord Shiva lies beneath her feet. Behind this fierce depiction of Goddess Kali lie centuries-old myths, religious beliefs and profound symbolism.
Hindus across Bangladesh are celebrating Kali Puja, also known as Shyama Puja, on Sunday, the new moon night of the Hindu month of Kartik.
One of the major religious festivals of Sanatan Dharma, Kali Puja is dedicated to Goddess Kali, who embodies divine power and the destruction of evil. Devotees light lamps, decorate temples and homes, and offer prayers seeking her blessings for protection, peace and prosperity.
The name ‘Kali’ is derived from the Sanskrit word ‘Kala’, meaning time, and is also associated with the colour black. In Hindu belief, Goddess Kali is a powerful manifestation of the Divine Mother, symbolising both creation and destruction.
Several stories in Hindu scriptures describe the emergence of Goddess Kali. One of the best-known accounts is associated with the demon Raktabija. According to Hindu mythology, Raktabija had received a boon that every drop of his blood that touched the ground would give rise to another demon identical to him. This made him virtually impossible for the gods to defeat.
To protect the gods from his growing power, Goddess Durga entered the battlefield. However, each time Raktabija was wounded, more demons emerged from the drops of his blood.
Faced with this challenge, Goddess Kali emerged from Durga's anger. She began drinking Raktabija's blood before it could reach the ground, preventing the creation of more demons. She eventually defeated him.
The story highlights Kali's role as the destroyer of evil and the protector of the universe.
One of the most striking features of Goddess Kali is her dark or deep blue complexion. She is also known as Shyama, meaning dark-coloured.
According to religious interpretations, her dark appearance represents the infinite nature of the universe and the power that transcends all colours and forms. Just as the vast sky has no visible boundaries, Kali's power is believed to be limitless.
Her dark complexion also reflects her association with Mahakala, or the supreme power of time.
Goddess Kali is commonly depicted wearing a garland of severed human heads around her neck. This striking feature carries several symbolic meanings.
One interpretation is that the garland represents the destruction of ego, ignorance and worldly attachments. Some religious traditions also associate the heads with the letters of the Sanskrit alphabet.
The imagery reminds devotees of the impermanence of human life and the futility of worldly pride.
In many traditional depictions, Kali also wears a belt of severed human hands around her waist.
The hands are often interpreted as symbols of human actions and their consequences. In Hindu philosophy, karma, or the consequences of one's actions, plays a central role in human life.
The belt is also seen as a reminder of the transient nature of worldly identity and attachment.
In traditional depictions, Kali holds a sword in one hand and a severed head in another.
The sword symbolises the destruction of evil, ignorance and injustice, while the severed head represents the elimination of ego and false pride.
Her other hands are often shown in gestures of blessing and protection, reflecting her dual role as a fierce destroyer of evil and a compassionate protector of her devotees.
Perhaps the most familiar and intriguing feature of Goddess Kali's image is Lord Shiva lying beneath her feet.
According to a popular mythological account, after defeating the demons, Kali became so enraged that she began a destructive dance, threatening to disrupt the balance of the universe.
Alarmed by the prospect of universal destruction, the gods turned to Lord Shiva for help. To stop her, Shiva lay down in her path. As Kali continued dancing, she unknowingly stepped on his chest.
Realising that she had stepped on her husband, Kali became embarrassed and stuck out her tongue.
This story is commonly cited to explain why Kali is depicted standing on Shiva with her tongue extended.
A deeper philosophical interpretation sees Shiva as the embodiment of pure consciousness and Kali as the manifestation of energy or power. Their union symbolises the relationship between consciousness and the dynamic force that sustains creation.
Goddess Kali is often depicted with long, flowing hair and without conventional clothing. This form is known as Digambari, meaning one whose clothing is the directions or the sky.
According to religious interpretations, her appearance represents freedom from worldly restrictions and social conventions. As the embodiment of infinite cosmic power, she cannot be confined by material boundaries.
Unlike many other Hindu festivals, Kali Puja is traditionally performed at night, particularly on the new moon night of Kartik.
According to religious belief, the darkness of the night represents the struggle between light and darkness, while the worship of Kali symbolises the destruction of evil and the awakening of divine power.
Devotees light oil lamps and candles in their homes and temples, creating an atmosphere of devotion and celebration.
Red hibiscus flowers hold a special place in Kali Puja. Devotees traditionally offer them to the goddess because the colour red is associated with strength, courage and power.
As Kali is worshipped as the embodiment of divine energy, the red hibiscus is considered a particularly fitting offering.
Kali worship has a long history in Bengal, particularly through the Shaktism tradition, which regards the Divine Mother as the supreme power.
Krishnananda Agamavagisha, a Tantric scholar from Nabadwip, is traditionally credited with popularising the worship of Goddess Kali through idols in Bengal.
During the 18th century, Raja Krishnachandra of Nadia is also believed to have played an important role in popularising Kali Puja. Later, wealthy landlords and influential families helped spread the festival across different parts of Bengal.
The devotional songs of Ramprasad Sen played a significant role in shaping the Bengali people's relationship with Goddess Kali. Through his compositions, Kali became more than a powerful deity; she emerged as a loving mother to whom devotees could express their hopes, fears and deepest emotions.
The spiritual practices of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa further strengthened the tradition of Kali worship in Bengal.
Kali Puja and Diwali are both observed on the new moon night of Kartik, but their principal forms of worship differ across regions.
In many parts of India, Diwali is associated with the worship of Goddess Lakshmi, the deity of wealth and prosperity. In Bengal and several eastern regions, devotees traditionally worship Goddess Kali on this night.
The word ‘Diwali’ means a row of lamps. Lighting lamps symbolises the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil.

item.title: The future of biodiversity relies on shared consensus
item.description:
Governments, civil society, scientists, youth, academia, artists, and media professionals gathered under the theme of 'Taking Action for Nature' at COP17 Armenia to bring about collective action on biodiversity protection and nature restoration.
Reviewing targets and protocols
COP17 Armenia conducted the first global review of the collective implementation progress of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). The KMGBF is set on 23 global biodiversity targets which are to be completed by 2030 in line with the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS).
Targets two and three, restoring 30% of all degraded ecosystems and conserving and effectively managing 30% of land, waters, and seas, respectively, took precedence in the KMGBF discussions. There has also been significant discourse on how KMGBF can be financed, how actors and stakeholders responsible for it can be accountable, and how its credibility can be ensured.
Strengthening biosafety by monitoring living modified organisms (LMO), reduction of invasive alien species, compliance and accountability, monitoring and evaluation, and ensuring gender equality and gender-responsive approach for biodiversity action were also discussed.
There was little difference in technical opinion on biodiversity protection, but there is hesitation in resource mobilization and funding implementation.
These conversations generated three critical questions:
The commitment to address these grand questions is there, but the scale, strength, and pace of the decisions are not enough.
One reason is the slow implementation of the National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAP) adopted by countries around the world. Another reason is the current economic and geopolitical trend. Their connection to biodiversity damage is not talked about enough.
The current global biodiversity funding gap stands at $700 billion. The GEF-9 Replenishment was announced, where new countries pledged close to $4.4bn. This barely scratches the surface of the gap. The CALI Fund adopted in COP16 Cali, Colombia garnered a lot of attention. It was initially created to collect private-sector contributions from industries that rely on genetic data in nature, for example big pharma, biotech companies, cosmetics giants, etc.
However, voluntary contributions have been measly. No major corporation contributed to the CALI Fund. Participants mainly talked about ensuring fair and equitable commercialisation and benefit-sharing of genetic data.
The polarity of financing perspectives is a recurring challenge that raises questions. Developing countries seek international finance to do the work. Developed countries, on the other hand, urged diversification of funding sources.
But how can we generate financial mechanisms that ensure direct access to local communities? How can we combine grants, loans, and other financial instruments to develop these mechanisms? How can we achieve more transparency in these processes?
The rights of nature and people
Target 18 of the KMGBF, which is reducing incentives and subsidies harmful for biodiversity by at least $500bn (for example phasing out pesticides) and introducing positive incentives without affecting biodiversity was up for debate and requires great political will.
This also applies to biodiversity-protected areas. There are calls to ensure improved and practical ecosystem development, biodiversity protection coordinated with livelihoods, community rights, and equitable governance.
One way is to acknowledge the legal rights of nature. Advocates explained how ecosystems and species have legal rights just like humans. This puts nature as a living entity at equal legal footing with humans, not as their property, such as Panama's Rights of Nature Law adopted in 2023.
Corporations harming these rights would be violating law. Such perspectives and laws can better support conservation and biodiversity protection, but inclusive implementation with women, youth, and indigenous communities is important here.
Aligning actions around the Rio Conventions
Integrating climate action and biodiversity action without duplicating mandates is fundamental if we are to address all three Rio Conventions -- climate change, desertification, and biodiversity.There was no structured discourse on Rio synergy in the conference.
There were talks about carbon trading and how local communities can participate and benefit from carbon trading marketplaces. If their ownership, stake, and decision-making remain, they can manage natural resources best without overexploitation. It will allow countries to maintain the carbon credit trade and reduce emissions sustainably.
For Bangladesh to make use of this market, mangrove restoration and wetland conservation are great areas to start.
The use of technology and AI in developing biodiversity information systems was met with optimism. Armenia and Colombia jointly committed to finance endangered species conservation through private sector engagement. There is hope to achieve all 23 targets by 2030, but things still do not look too good.
From a Global South perspective, we raised concerns about how biodiversity conservation should complement livelihoods, respect community experiences, and engage people of faith.
We must consider the Rio synergies, and we must ensure multi-stakeholder governance and multilateral cooperation. We urged governments and experts to create a structured method to measure impact on ecosystem recovery, species conservation status, livelihood resilience outcomes, and equitable benefit sharing.
Science should be able to influence policy-making and economics and create tripartite solutions. We have committed to nature, to the world, and to the people with the KMGBF. Without its implementation, we are failing ourselves.
Will the global review lead to stronger, measurable action before 2030? Will biodiversity finance and governance genuinely empower local communities?
The world does not need another declaration of concern about biodiversity loss. While we saw great progress in technical aspects, the success of that progress truly depends on political consensus.
If governments together can adopt these technical perspectives and put them into proper funding pathways, policy, and practice, there is hope for the future of biodiversity.
Kazi Amdadul Hoque is the Senior Director, Strategic Planning & Head of Climate Action at Friendship.

item.title: The muddying of the waters
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir, when answering journalists’ questions on various serious subjects, often tries to create a little humor with some sarcasm and mockery.
Recently, Kabir was asked whether former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had applied for a passport to return to the country. The question can’t be called entirely reasonable, since there has been nothing to suggest that Hasina has applied for a passport at all.
In other words, the person about whom the passport question is being asked has herself said nothing about a passport. Anyway, if a journalist is curious, they will naturally ask, and a responsible official could be expected to give a proper answer.
The state minister said he knows nothing about a passport. Of course, he wouldn’t, because Sheikh Hasina has said nothing about a passport or a travel pass. Kabir, however, did not stop there.
“Is she going to come here to visit her in-laws’ home in Rangpur, that I should give her a passport, and she’ll come with the passport?” He described the matter as “laughable.” Then he laid out the government’s position in his own words.
“Sheikh Hasina is a fugitive terrorist. A dictator, a runaway terrorist,” he said.
Kabir’s choice of words here is quite interesting. Humayun Kabir is a Britain-based expatriate, so he knows well what “terrorist” means in the Western world. There, “terrorist” mainly means Islamist militants (although in the United States some armed white supremacist groups are designated as “domestic terrorist” organizations). Here a suspicion remains that, by labeling Hasina a “terrorist,” the minister wants to create an image of her in the minds of Westerners.
On bringing Hasina back from India, Kabir stood firm on his earlier position. “We have an active extradition treaty for catching terrorists, for catching criminals,” he said. “To catch terrorists and criminals, you don’t need a passport; they are handed over.”
He is right about this. The very purpose of the extradition treaty between Bangladesh and India is to arrest each other’s “terrorists” and “criminals” and send them back.
The problem lies elsewhere. Does India see Sheikh Hasina as a “terrorist” or “criminal” at all?
From the answer that Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi recently gave to a university student’s question at an event, no one should have any doubt that the Indian government, far from considering Sheikh Hasina a terrorist or criminal, treats her with considerable respect. Throughout his entire statement, Trivedi addressed the former PM as “Hasinaji.” Those with even the slightest idea of Indian social customs know that in that country, no responsible person adds “ ji ” to the name of a criminal or terrorist.
Is a passport a citizen’s right?
Trivedi had said that Hasina came to India on August 5, 2024 as the prime minister of Bangladesh. He also said the Indian Air Force did not “rescue” her from Ganabhaban. It was Bangladesh’s own military that took her to Delhi for her safety.
If India does not see Hasina as a “terrorist” or “criminal,” there is considerable room for doubt about whether the extradition treaty, however active, would apply in her case.
There is a second problem with Humayun Kabir’s statement. The government’s spokesperson and the Prime Minister’s Adviser on Policy and Strategy, Zahed Ur Rahman, said something slightly different a day earlier.
When he was asked multiple questions on the same subject at his regular press briefing, he did not directly rule out the possibility of giving Hasina a passport. He said he knows Hasina has made no such application, and that the government has no plan sitting ready.
“If it were the case that she (Hasina) had asked for it (a passport), then what the government would do, I think it is better to keep that to answer at that time.”
Rahman’s reply lightly touches on another aspect, whose importance is immense. He brought up the issue of citizenship, and he spoke of “this state,” that is, the state that was founded under the leadership of Hasina’s father.
Leaving the country and coming back is the constitutional right of all citizens of “this state” -- getting the document needed for travel, that is, a passport, is also their right. But under Bangladeshi law, in certain cases a citizen’s passport can be canceled, and they can be barred from leaving the country, and likewise an application for a passport can be rejected.
But canceling or rejecting a passport is all done to stop someone from leaving the country. The matter of returning to the country from abroad remains somewhat murky.
Extradition versus return
Hundreds of cases have been filed against Sheikh Hasina; one or two have been “tried” in her absence, and she has even been given the death sentence. The government considers Hasina a “fugitive,” so surely the government would want her to return and come under the country’s law?
Since Hasina has expressed a wish to return voluntarily in December, that apparently seems the easiest and quickest path. On the other hand, the extradition that Humayun Kabir speaks of, which Zahed Ur Rahman dramatically explains as “we will bring her by catching her,” is a long legal process; nobody can say how many months, or even years, the extradition process might take.
And even after the process ends, there is no guarantee that the Indian government will actually hand Sheikh Hasina over to face the death sentence.
Against this background, if the government chooses the long extradition process as the only road, and dismisses the possibility of a quick return with some absurd remark, then only one conclusion can be drawn: The government in fact does not want Sheikh Hasina to return to the country. That is, the government does not want the verdict in Hasina’s concluded trial to be carried out.
Listening to the state minister, it does not seem that Hasina’s presence in the country is desirable to the government. There could be two reasons.
First, in the current situation, the government has neither the political courage nor the strength to carry out the verdict against Sheikh Hasina.
Second, Hasina’s return would, on the one hand, revive the Awami League, and on the other, push the anger of Jamaat-e-Islami and the NCP to its peak. Perhaps the BNP lacks the confidence to face this two-sided political challenge.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.

item.title: Father loses one son, younger child on life support
item.description:
In a desperate bid to save his nine-year-old son, Mohammad Kabir rushed him from one hospital to another, seeking treatment at four different facilities. Days passed with the child battling for life in intensive care. But despite every effort, the father could not save his son Nur Mohammad Arafat.
Arafat died last Friday while undergoing treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) of Chittagong Maa-O-Shishu Hospital. Yet, before Kabir could come to terms with the loss and return home after burying his son, another nightmare unfolded. His 10-month-old younger son, Mohammad Abu Bakkar, was also fighting for his life in the ICU of the same hospital. He was placed on life support on Saturday morning.
According to family members, Arafat was a third-grade student at Hillview Public School in Panchlaish. Around 18 to 20 days ago, he developed a fever, accompanied by vomiting and cough. After a series of medical tests, doctors diagnosed him with measles, dengue and pneumonia.
Kabir said Arafat was first admitted to Southern Hospital, where he received treatment for four days. As his condition worsened, he was transferred to Marine City Hospital, where he spent two days in the ICU. He was then moved to Imperial Hospital for another four days of intensive care. However, his condition showed no signs of improvement. Last Monday, Arafat was admitted to the ICU of Chittagong Maa-O-Shishu Hospital. He died there on Friday and was buried at Momenbagh graveyard in the city later that day.
But the family's ordeal was far from over. Kabir said his younger son Abu Bakkar had also contracted measles, dengue and pneumonia. The infant had been taken to three hospitals for intensive care, but his condition continued to deteriorate. On Saturday morning, doctors placed him on life support.
“I saw my younger son this morning. He is on life support, and the doctors cannot give me any assurance. They say they are doing everything they can. But I can see that my child can neither speak nor move. He is lying motionless. Only his heartbeat remains,” Kabir said.
“How much more can a father endure? I have just returned after burying one son. I cannot bear the thought of losing the other,” he added.
Professor Dr Didarul Alam, head of the Paediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU) and a paediatric specialist at Chittagong Maa-O-Shishu Hospital, said both children had been brought to the hospital in extremely critical condition.
“Even so, we have not given up. We still have hope. When a child contracts dengue and measles simultaneously, multiple vital organs may fail to function properly. That is what has happened in Abu Bakkar’s case. As doctors, we are making every possible effort to save his life,” he said.
Kabir lives with his wife and two sons in a rented house in the city's Hillview area. He works as a goods loader at a private company, while his wife, Amena Begum, 29, is a homemaker.
The cost of treatment for both children has already exceeded Tk2.5 lakh to Tk3 lakh, Kabir said. After exhausting his savings, he borrowed money from relatives and colleagues to continue their treatment.
Now, the father finds himself caught between the unbearable grief of losing one son and the agonising uncertainty of whether he can save the other. Having exhausted his savings and borrowed beyond his means, he continues to hold on to hope as his youngest child battles for life in the ICU.

item.title: Nearly 300 families wiped out in road accidents over 6 years and 10 months
item.description:
Road Safety Foundation (RSF) in an analytical report on Sunday said nearly 300 families have been completely wiped out in road accidents over the past 6 years and 10 months.
Talking to BSS, foundation's executive director Saidur Rahman said the trend of entire families being killed together in road accidents is increasing.
An analysis of road accidents from 2020 to October 2026 shows a growing number of incidents in which entire families, or multiple members of the same family, have been killed while travelling on motorcycles, auto-rickshaws, private cars, microbuses, ambulances, and buses, he added.
Rahman said they prepared this report based on information collected from nine national daily newspapers, 17 online news portals, electronic media, and its own database.
There were 193 incidents in which both husband and wife were killed while travelling on motorcycles, and 159 incidents in which a father and child were killed.
In other words, 386 people (husbands and wives) were killed in 193 motorcycle accidents, while 318 people (fathers and children) were killed in 159 motorcycle accidents.
A total of 1,728 people were killed in 525 road crashes involving battery-run three-wheeled rickshaw accidents locally called auto-rickshaw.
The number of incidents in which multiple members of the same family were killed while travelling in auto-rickshaws is as follows: 2 family members killed in 211 incidents, 3 family members killed in 118 incidents, 4 family members killed: 92 incidents, 5 family members killed in 53 incidents, 6 family members killed in 38 incidents and 7 family members killed in 13 incidents
The number of incidents in which multiple members of the same family were killed while travelling in microbuses is as follows: 2 family members killed in 48 incidents, 3 family members killed in 46 incidents, 4 family members killed in 39 incidents, 5 family members killed in 28 incidents, 6 family members killed in 20 incidents, 11 family members killed in 4 incidents and 14 family members killed 1 incident. A total of 708 people were killed in 186 road crashes involving motorbuses.
The number of incidents in which multiple members of the same family were killed while travelling in private cars is as follows: 2 family members killed in 34 incidents, 3 family members killed in 31 incidents, 4 family members killed in 24 incidents, 5 family members killed in 19 incidents.
A total of 352 people were killed in 108 accidents.
The number of incidents in which multiple members of the same family were killed while travelling in ambulances is as follows: 2 family members killed in 11 incidents, 3 family members killed in 15 incidents, 4 family members killed in 9 incidents, 5 family members killed in 7 incidents and 8 family members killed in 3 incidents. A total of 162 people were killed in 45 ambulance accidents.
The number of incidents in which multiple members of the same family were killed while travelling on buses is as follows: 2 family members killed in 17 incidents, 3 family members killed in 9 incidents, 4 family members killed in 6 incidents
A total of 85 people were killed in 32 bus accidents.
In one incident, four members of the same family were killed when a pickup van lost control and overturned.
The foundation found out several causes of road crashes including the growing tendency of entire families to travel together for work or leisure, the operation of auto-rickshaws on highways, the lack of roadworthiness and fitness certification of most microbuses and ambulances, the lack of driving skills among microbus and ambulance drivers, along with driving for prolonged periods without adequate rest, failure to use standard-quality helmets and reckless motorcycle driving, the tendency to violate traffic laws.
It gave a set of recommendations including wearing high quality helmets by motorcyclists and pillions and driving motor vehicles in compliance with traffic laws.
It suggested that road dividers and service roads should be constructed on all highways, safe road designs should be developed to prevent rural roads from connecting directly to highways, the movement of vehicles on roads and highways must be properly monitored, the institutional effectiveness, transparency, and accountability of relevant organizations must be ensured, educational and public awareness programs should be conducted to improve the knowledge and capabilities of road users.

item.title: Crude bomb hurled at private car in Mirpur-1
item.description:
A crude bomb exploded after being thrown at a private car in front of Sony Hall in the capital’s Mirpur-1 area on Sunday night.
The incident occurred around 8:30pm on Sunday. No casualties were reported.
Mirpur Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Hafizur Rahman said a crude bomb was hurled at the car and exploded in front of Sony Hall.
He added that the attack was reportedly carried out by individuals arriving on a motorcycle. Police are working to identify those involved.

item.title: Bangladesh advance to SAFF semis after Bhutan-Sri Lanka draw
item.description:
Bangladesh have secured a place in the semi-finals of the SAFF Championship 2026 after Bhutan and Sri Lanka played out a 2-2 draw in their Group A encounter at the National Stadium in Dhaka on Sunday.
The men in red and green defeated Bhutan 1-0 in their opening and only group match to secure three points, enough to book their place in the last four following the draw.
Bangladesh will face Sri Lanka in their concluding group-stage fixture on Wednesday, with the winner set to advance to the semi-finals as Group A champions.
Bhutan took the lead in the 34th minute as Chencho Gyeltshen split the Sri Lankan defence down the left flank before delivering a cross into the danger zone. Dawa Tshering found the back of the net after Kinga Wangchuk's attempt was blocked.
Sri Lanka responded quickly, with Oliver James equalising in the 36th minute through a long-range effort into the bottom corner. Ahmed Waseem then put Sri Lanka ahead in the 43rd minute with a low header following Oliver's cross.
Chencho had a chance to restore parity from the penalty spot in the 67th minute, but Sri Lankan goalkeeper Sujan Perera dived to his right to save the Bhutanese forward's effort.
The Bhutanese star, however, made amends in the 76th minute, firing home to secure a crucial point for his side.
Bhutan could still progress to the semi-finals if Bangladesh defeat Sri Lanka by at least two goals on Wednesday.
Earlier in the day, Najeeb Ullah scored a brace as Pakistan defeated Maldives 3-0 in their second Group B fixture to become the first team to reach the semi-finals.
The victory was enough for Pakistan to advance to the last four despite their 3-2 defeat to India in the tournament opener, with their goal difference from the two matches proving decisive.
Aroon Abdullah converted a penalty to give Pakistan the lead in the fourth minute.
Najeeb doubled the advantage five minutes later with a composed finish following a cross from Junaid Ahmed Shah.
The forward struck again in the 24th minute, drifting into the box to find the net and put Pakistan firmly in control.
Maldives had an opportunity to reduce the deficit in the 52nd minute, but substitute Ali Fasir struck the post after being set up by Ibrahim Mahudhee Hussain.
Pakistan also came close to extending their lead on a couple of occasions, with their powerful attempts narrowly missing the target.
With the victory, Pakistan completed their Group B fixtures, while Maldives and India still have a match to play to determine the other semi-finalist.

item.title: PM urges new BCS officers to serve people with honesty, efficiency and humanity
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday urged newly recruited civil servants to serve people with honesty, efficiency and human values, stressing that no citizen should face harassment while seeking services from government offices.
“Regardless of a citizen's age, you must ensure that they do not face any kind of harassment when they come to your offices seeking assistance,” he said.
The prime minister was addressing the closing ceremony of the 81st Foundation Training Course for newly recruited BCS officers at the Bangladesh Public Administration Training Centre (BPATC) in Savar.
Addressing the officers, he said they were about to begin a new chapter in their professional lives after completing their academic studies and receiving practical training.
Tarique congratulated them on completing the four-month course and wished them success in their future careers.
He said an efficient, honest and humane administration was essential for the overall success of any government.
“An administration with efficiency, honesty and human values not only enriches an individual officer but also strengthens the state and the government,” the prime minister said.
He said the newly trained officers would join different cadres, including administration, foreign affairs, agriculture, taxation, education and information, and their duties might vary depending on their respective fields.
“But whatever your cadre or workplace, your first and foremost identity is that you are officers of the public administration, and you are there to serve the people,” Tarique said.
He said he did not want to give them a lengthy lecture on what they should or should not do, as they were already aware of their responsibilities. “What matters most is your willingness to put that knowledge into practice,” he added.
Referring to the principle of treating others as one would like to be treated, the prime minister urged the officers to show citizens the same consideration and cooperation they would expect when seeking assistance themselves.
He said government officials must perform their duties within the limits of the law, stressing that humane behaviour towards service seekers was also equally important in a modern state and administration.
Giving an example, Tarique said an officer should not simply tell a citizen to correct mistakes in an application; rather, the officer should clearly identify the errors and guide the person on where and how to get them corrected. “The country’s people expect not only instructions and orders from you but also humanity,” he said.
He also advised the officers not to compromise their professional integrity and efficiency in pursuit of preferred postings or promotions.
The prime minister said being mentally prepared to serve in any position and any part of the country was a sign of true professionalism. “Just as a government is not permanent, no position in the public administration is permanent for anyone,” he said.
He said he did not personally consider it wrong for government officials to support a particular political party, but such support should be reflected at the ballot box, not in government offices.
Tarique acknowledged that the government was implementing its political agenda through the administration, but said it was doing so based on the electoral mandate given by the people.
He said his party had placed an election manifesto before the people before the national election and that voters had endorsed it.
“The election manifesto has now become the people's manifesto and their document. So, implementing it is the responsibility of the present government,” the prime minister said, urging the officers to carry out the necessary administrative work sincerely.
He also stressed the need to reduce delays in public administration and make government services easier and more citizen-friendly.
Tarique said a positive attitude among government officials and employees was often more effective than administrative initiatives alone in improving public services.
At the end of his speech, he urged the officers to pay greater attention to environmental protection and cleanliness, saying keeping homes, offices and public spaces clean would help build a cleaner country for future generations.
The prime minister handed over certificates to 10 top-performing officers among the participants of the four-month training course.

item.title: Customers receive over Tk2.5cr in insurance claims for dengue
item.description:
MetLife Bangladesh customers received over Tk2.5 crore in dengue claims between January and October 2026, helping families meet medical expenses and stay financially secure.
For many families, a dengue infection means several days in hospital, repeated tests, and medication, with costs that arrive without warning.
The on-time claim payments have provided meaningful financial relief to recipients, helping them focus on recovery and manage hospital expenses.
These claims highlight the importance of planning early for unexpected situations.
They also show that the benefits of insurance are not limited to the time of death but are also available to people while they are living.

item.title: Islami Bank holds workshop to prevent fraud in agent banking
item.description:
A training workshop titled “Training on Prevention of Fraud and Forgery at Agent Banking Outlets” was recently organized by the Cox’s Bazar Branch of Islami Bank Bangladesh PLC in coordination with the Agent Banking Division, focusing on preventing fraud in agent banking, ensuring compliance and improving the quality of secure banking services.
Md Iqbal Mohasin, director and head of the Financial Inclusion Department (FID) of Bangladesh Bank attended the workshop as chief guest.
Md Ali Hossain, additional director (FID) of Bangladesh Bank, and Abul Laise Mohd. Khaled, head of the agent banking division of Islami Bank Bangladesh PLC, attended as special guests.
Abdul Naser, executive vice president and head of Chattogram south zone of the bank, presided over the program.
Mohammad Burhan Uddin Khan, head of Cox’s Bazar branch, delivered the welcome speech.
The workshop covered agent banking policies, roles and responsibilities, compliance requirements, fraud detection and preventive measures.
Emphasis was placed on strict adherence to regulatory guidelines, cautious handling of transactions and enhancing the skills of relevant personnel to ensure customer trust and security in agent banking services.

item.title: Bank Asia, Asia Insurance to ensure insurance coverage with two-wheeler loans
item.description:
Bank Asia PLC has signed a strategic Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Asia Insurance PLC to offer robust insurance coverage for buyers availing two-wheeler loan facilities, making motorcycle purchases more convenient and accessible for prospective buyers.
The partnership will also encompass joint marketing initiatives, customer engagement programs and promotional activities to enhance customer awareness and facilitate access to financial and insurance services.
The MoU was signed in a ceremony held at Rupayan Trade Centre, Bangla Motor, Dhaka recently.
Md Zahed Chowdhury, executive vice president & head of assets, retail banking division of Bank Asia, and Md Imam Shaheen, chief executive officer & managing director of Asia Insurance, signed the agreement on behalf of their respective organizations.
Through this partnership, motorcycle buyers will have access to convenient financing facilities along with suitable insurance coverage for their vehicles.

item.title: Tuku: All must work together for Bangladesh’s development
item.description:
State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salahuddin Tuku on Sunday called for collective efforts to ensure the country's overall development and progress, saying everyone must put Bangladesh first.
He made the call while addressing a discussion at Shaheed Smriti Poura Udyan in Tangail town on Sunday morning, marking 55th National Cooperatives Day.
Quoting the prime minister's slogan, “We will work, we will build the country, Bangladesh comes first,” Tuku said everyone must work together, keeping the country's interests at heart, to build a prosperous and peaceful Bangladesh.
He also stressed that people from all walks of life must fulfil their responsibilities and work towards building a drug-free society. Highlighting the role of cooperatives, the state minister called for establishing small cooperative societies at the grassroots level to organize people and strengthen their economic position.
“Cooperatives can promote mutual cooperation, unity and self-reliance. They can also play a vital role in improving rural living standards and creating employment opportunities,” he said.
Later, Tuku distributed loan cheques among cooperative members and visited a fair showcasing cooperative products.

item.title: Minister: Sheikh Hasina will never return to Bangladesh
item.description:
Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Azam Khan on Sunday said Sheikh Hasina will never return to Bangladesh, warning that attempts to destabilise the country through sabotage will not be tolerated.
“We want Hasina to return to face trial and go to prison over the numerous allegations of genocide against her. But she will never return. Instead, she will spread rumours, destabilise the country and incite Awami League leaders and activists to engage in sabotage,” he said.
He made the remarks while speaking at a discussion meeting, organized by the Sakhipur upazila BNP on Sunday afternoon, marking the National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
The minister said Bangladesh had no room for sabotage and would move forward towards democracy and development.
He also criticised opposition parties for staging frequent demonstrations and issuing threats and ultimatums. While the prime minister was making efforts at home and abroad to tackle the fuel crisis, thousands of vehicles were being brought out in processions, wasting fuel, he said, calling the practice condemnable.
Ahmed Azam Khan urged the government to be given five years to govern, saying the next election would be held after that period under a system ensuring people's voting rights.
“There will be no election under a partisan government. Voting will take place during the day, not at night, and no one will be allowed to cast another person's vote,” he said. Urging opposition parties to exercise restraint, he warned that people would reject those whose actions disrupted development and created instability.

item.title: Hodge century leaves Bangladesh facing uphill battle to level Test series
item.description:
Kavem Hodge smashed a scintillating century to put West Indies in a dominating position in the second and final cricket Test against Bangladesh today as the visitors moved closer to series sweep at Sylhet International Cricket Stadium.
Hodge's unbeaten 140, complemented by half-centuries from Kevin Wickham (78) and opener Brandon King (61), propelled West Indies to 345-3 at stumps on Day 4, extending their overall lead to 315 runs.
With just one day remaining, West Indies are firmly in control of the contest and well placed to set Bangladesh a daunting target in the fourth innings. From this point, West Indies in fact remain the only team in a position to push for a victory.
Bangladesh bowlers struggled to make an impact throughout the day after West Indies resumed their second innings at 7 without loss, looking to build on the 30-run deficit from the first innings.
King and Joshua Da Silva put on 85 runs for the opening wicket before left-arm spinner Taijul Islam broke through, trapping Da Silva leg-before for 36.
King, meanwhile, continued his fluent batting, reaching his sixth Test half-century before falling to off-spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz after making 61. His 84-ball knock featured 10 fours and a six.
The two quick wickets gave Bangladesh a brief opportunity to put the visitors under pressure through spin. However, Hodge and debutant Wickham quickly took control, using their feet effectively to sweep the spinners with precision.
The pair added 131 runs for the third wicket, taking West Indies into a commanding position.
Wickham, who scored 61 in the first innings, registered his second half-century of the match on debut, reaching the landmark off 68 balls with a boundary through extra cover.
He looked set for a maiden Test century but fell for 78 when he casually chipped a Taijul delivery straight back to the bowler.
Taijul finished the day with 2-118, while Bangladesh's other bowlers found it difficult to contain the West Indies batters.
Hodge, however, remained untroubled and continued his attacking approach to bring up his third Test century off 142 balls, sweeping Taijul towards square leg for a single.
He was unbeaten on 140 at stumps, while Amir Jangoo, who scored a century in the first innings, was batting on 20.
The day's play was eventually called off due to bad light, leaving Bangladesh with a formidable challenge heading into the final day.
Earlier, Hasan Mahmud claimed 6-90 to bowl West Indies out for 356 in their first innings. Bangladesh responded with 386, securing a crucial 30-run lead, largely thanks to Towhid Hridoy monumental 242 not out.

item.title: Gaza: Rains add misery to humanitarian catastrophe
item.description:
Heavy rains sweeping across parts of the Middle East this week have flooded tens of thousands of tents in Gaza’s displaced persons’ camps.
According to authorities in the enclave, at least 70,000 tents have been flooded over the past day, where tens of thousands of people took shelter.
No fatalities had been reported, although some people were injured.
Some of the tents have been washed away due to the weather, with mattresses and blankets soaked with water.
More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza’s 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters due to Israel’s war in the enclave.
UN data says some 80% of the enclave’s structures have been damaged during the war, with two-thirds destroyed, leaving Gaza’s residents — many of whom were displaced multiple times during the war between Israel and Hamas — to either live in tents or risk their lives and seek shelter in buildings that could be on the verge of collapse.
The Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs in Palestine released a statement appealing for humanitarian aid for the Gaza Strip due to the situation.
According to the committee, some 950,000 people are living in areas “vulnerable to flooding,” with more than 400,000 living in areas of “high levels of risk.”
“Heavy rainfall is compounding an already catastrophic humanitarian situation, leaving displaced families and those who have lost their homes exposed to the elements and deprived of the most basic necessities of life,” the statement said.
A UN commission of inquiry, as well as many leading human rights organizations, have accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza. Israel has rejected the accusation, saying its army is acting in accordance with international law.

item.title: As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?
item.description:
With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya’s marketing video is clear: Turkiye, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.
Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkiye’s first lady calling climate change “one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.”
From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkiye is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they’ll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.
Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe’s main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.
And in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.
Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.
The global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there’s been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.
Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.
David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3 and 3.5°C.
If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6°C. It’s a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.
“There’s no question that we could be doing more,” said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year’s summit.
All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year’s negotiations.
“It’s like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody’s hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it,” said Victor. “We have to look at it for what it is: It’s a place where people talk about stuff.”
Instead of waiting for all COP member states to come to an agreement, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called “clubs” — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.
“The Paris process is important. It has to go forward,” he told DW. “But all the work is going to be done in clubs.”
An example of this approach was last April’s first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.
Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.
With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkiye and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.
A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries’ energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.
Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark new momentum in the “global phaseout of fossil fuels.”
It’s wouldn’t just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.
Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren’t interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they’ve repeatedly blocked any final agreements including phaseout plans.
Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.
Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.
That’s where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.
But where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.
The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.
“The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what’s needed,” said Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.
Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power, on which Germany and other industrialized nations rely to shape policy to fight climate change.
Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkiye’s push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.
For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.
When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.

item.title: Bobby Hajjaj: Govt aims to establish 'learning-outcome-based' education system
item.description:
State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj has said the government is working to develop a learning-outcome-based and children-friendly education system for the new 2028 curriculum, considering the age, capabilities, and learning needs of students.
In a recent interview with BSS, he discussed in detail the government's future action plans for the primary education sector, including ensuring the quality of primary education, expanding the nationwide mid-day meal programme, and integrating technology into the classroom.
Regarding the development of the primary education curriculum, Bobby Hajjaj said the government has begun the process of formulating a refined and improved curriculum, aligned with the age, capabilities, and learning needs of students.
The National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) has been entrusted with this task, he said.
The state minister said the new curriculum focuses on eliminating disparities in instructional hours across different schools, while also making teaching methods and learning materials for each subject more scientific, accessible and age-appropriate.
The government is working to create a joyful classroom environment where students can learn through play, he added.
By incorporating educational toys alongside textbooks, he said, teachers will be able to facilitate learning in a more accessible and engaging manner.
Also, he said, special emphasis is being placed on enhancing proficiency in Bangla, Mathematics, and English, as well as on the use of digital content and practical, hands-on learning activities.
There are also plans to encourage student participation in mathematics and science olympiads, as well as in cultural activities, he continued.
Bobby Hajjaj highlighted the "Mid-Day Meal" programme as a key government priority, aimed at maintaining student attendance and ensuring nutritional security.
He said the programme is currently ongoing successfully in 151 upazilas across the country.
A new Development Project Proforma (DPP) is being drafted to expand the programme to the remaining upazilas, he said, expressing optimism that by 2027, it will be possible to provide nutritious mid-day meals to every child in all government primary schools across the country.
About food quality and transparency in distribution, Bobby Hajjaj said the receipt and distribution of meals are being strictly supervised by 'mothers' committees', groups formed by the students' mothers.
Besides, a "zero-tolerance" policy is being implemented through regular monitoring at field level.
Referring to "One Teacher, One Tab" and "Smart Classroom" initiatives, the state minister said this is not merely a project for distributing devices.
In collaboration with major global technology firms, including Google, the government plans to develop a comprehensive digital ecosystem for classrooms in government primary schools, with tablets provided to teachers serving as the primary connecting link, he said.
He said this will function as part of an integrated central network, enabling real-time monitoring to identify whether a class is struggling to complete the syllabus or if students are facing difficulties in understanding specific topics.
In addition, the state minister said, for primary schools in remote areas lacking electricity, an initiative has been launched, in coordination with the Power Division, to install solar panels and ensure internet bandwidth.
The government is firmly committed to enhancing the quality of primary education through regular teacher training, Bobby Hajjaj said, adding: "The development of primary education extends beyond merely constructing school buildings or ensuring student attendance, while the most critical factor is whether every child attending school is truly learning."
Regarding the development of primary education, the state minister noted that to implement the desired reforms, a coordinated approach must be taken prioritising five key areas: curriculum, teachers, monitoring, infrastructure, and technology.
He explained that all aspects of primary education are closely interconnected.
"Achieving the desired success is not possible if one area is developed while others are neglected. So, comprehensive reform initiatives must be advanced based on ground-level realities and the input of relevant stakeholders," Bobby Hajjaj said.
Addressing the infrastructure of primary schools, said development should not be limited to the construction of buildings alone.
Classrooms, furniture, sanitation facilities, and access to safe drinking water must be tailored to the needs of children, he said.
Beyond ensuring a safe and children-friendly learning environment, infrastructure must be designed with consideration for the specific geographical realities of different regions, he said.
The state minister said in accordance with the specific directives of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, the government is putting emphasis on ensuring educational opportunities for every child in the country, fostering moral values, and equipping students with the skills necessary for their future careers.

item.title: Naogaon University adopts zero tolerance for ragging
item.description:
Naogaon University Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Mohammad Hasanath Ali has warned that no form of ragging will be tolerated on campus, particularly under the pretext of teaching manners to junior students.
He said senior students could treat their juniors to ice cream or cake and build friendships with them, but harassing or intimidating them in the name of teaching manners would invite strict disciplinary and legal action.
“I will not allow any junior student to become a victim of ragging. Those involved will face action, including cancellation of their studentship and legal proceedings, if necessary,” he said, reaffirming the university's zero-tolerance policy on ragging.
The vice-chancellor made the remarks at a programme marking the completion of the first-semester courses for students of the Law and Accounting departments on Sunday afternoon.
Prof Hasanath said the university aimed to become a quality institution and a model for other universities across the country.
He said the university had a digital library to facilitate research and urged faculty members to continue their research activities, assuring them of all necessary support from the administration.
He said the university needed to make significant progress by 2027 in land acquisition, land development, construction of boundary walls and the development of five specialised buildings.
He also urged the government to approve the Development Project Proposal (DPP) submitted by the university, expressing hope that the project would be approved soon to help fulfil the aspirations of the people of Naogaon.
Expressing confidence in government support, he said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman regularly enquired about the university's progress. He also acknowledged the role of university syndicate member Mir Shah-e-Alam in following up on its development.
Prof Hasanath said the university was gradually moving forward to fulfil its commitments to the people of Naogaon.
Among others, Pro-Vice-Chancellor Dr Mohammad Tarikul Islam, Kahaloo Upazila Nirbahi Officer Maliha Khanam, Accounting Department lecturer Sanjida Kabir and Law Department lecturer Zahidul Islam Sourav attended the programme.

item.title: 13-year-old madrasa student dies by suicide over TikTok row
item.description:
A 13-year-old madrasa student allegedly died by suicide in Gournadi upazila of Barisal after her mother reprimanded her for using TikTok instead of studying.
The deceased was a Class VII student at Sundardi Gausia Abedia Sunnia Madrasa. Her father lives in Italy.
Quoting family members, Gournadi Model police station OC Tarif Hasan Russell said deceased mother scolded her on Saturday afternoon, prompting her to hang herself from a beam in the kitchen while other family members were unaware.
She was rushed to the upazila health complex, where doctors declared her dead.
The OC said the body was handed over to the family as they had no complaints. Police have filed an unnatural death case.

item.title: Four crude bomb explosions reported at DU, two held
item.description:
Crude bomb explosions were reported at four locations on the Dhaka University (DU) campus on Sunday evening, while students detained two people allegedly attempting to set off another bomb near the Teacher-Student Centre (TSC).
The incidents took place around 6:30pm. Students later handed the two detainees over to the university’s proctorial team.
According to preliminary information, explosions occurred beside the university’s administrative building, at VC Chattar, in front of the Mukti O Gonotontro Toron near Nilkhet, and in the TSC area.
At the TSC, students detained two people while they were allegedly attempting to set off a cocktail. The device may have been thrown towards the area from the direction of Suhrawardy Udyan, according to initial reports.
DU Proctor Professor Mohammad Israfil Prang said students detained the two individuals following the incident near the TSC and handed them over to the proctorial team.
“They are being taken to the proctor’s office. We have already informed Shahbagh police. We are reviewing CCTV footage to understand what happened,” he said.
